source.title: Sparse Double Descent: Where Network Pruning Aggravates Overfitting
source.authors: Zhengqi He; Zeke Xie; Quanzhi Zhu; Zeng-Chang Qin

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own double-descent-like results in a new setting: increasing network sparsity through pruning, rather than increasing model size, epochs, or sample size. Its label-noise experiments also bear on V6's noise-dependence component.
record.gate_note: The paper varies pruning sparsity, not model size, training-set size, or training time as a double-descent axis. It does not test the original model-wise or data-wise curves. Its epoch plots show training dynamics but do not report an epoch-wise fall-rise-fall result. The study's distinct sparse-double-descent results and its label-noise dependence are recorded; cited results from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps capacity by iterative pruning (sparsity) instead of width or depth. It reports its own test-accuracy curves showing a fall-rise-fall shape, with the 'Critical Phase' placed at the interpolation threshold, where train accuracy starts to drop. Read as remaining parameter count, this is a new setting for model-wise double descent (V1). Its noise-rate sweep and no-noise controls bear on V6's noise dependence.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that, under label noise, increasing pruning sparsity yields sparse double descent: test performance worsens (Critical Phase), improves (Sweet Phase), then collapses. L2 learning distance correlates with this 'to a certain extent' and explains it better than minima flatness. Winning lottery tickets may not always win.
record.recipe_differences: The study iteratively prunes network weights and measures train/test accuracy against sparsity; it does not reproduce the original model-size, epoch, or sample-size sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported sparse-double-descent pattern varies with label-noise rate; the Critical Phase moves toward lower sparsity and the Sweet Phase toward higher sparsity as noise increases. The paper also reports the pattern across pruning strategies and retraining methods.

fits_no_version.finding: L2 distance from initialization peaks near the test-accuracy turning point on MNIST but not distinctly on CIFAR-100.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning distance from initialization tracks the sparse double-descent curve in some but not all settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Reinitialized pruned models still show sparse double descent, but with both the Critical and Sweet Phases shifted to lower sparsity. They can beat lottery tickets at some sparsities (Fig. 10, 33-34).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The location of the sparse double-descent peak depends on initialization of the pruned subnetwork.

record.problems: The main sparse-double-descent values are presented in plots rather than as numeric tables. The evidence emphasizes synthetic label noise and pruning sparsity; it does not directly establish the original model-size, epoch-wise, or sample-size claims. The paper reports repeated runs and mean and standard deviation for its MNIST and other dataset experiments.
record.rows_left_out: Additional figure-only sparse-pruning curves across pruning strategies, retraining methods, datasets, noise types, and architectures appear in Figures 2-3 and 13-30. They were not transcribed individually to keep the record concise; the paper describes the sparse pattern as recurring across these settings. Training-dynamics plots in Figures 6 and 35-36 were not recorded as epoch-wise double-descent results because the paper does not describe them as showing that pattern.

untested.parts: Model size is not grown by width or depth. Capacity is varied only by pruning a fixed architecture.
No epoch-wise fall-rise-fall test. Training curves (Figs 35-36) are used only to show convergence.
Only deep networks are pruned; there are no non-deep model classes.
No effective-complexity measure is tested across the size, epoch and sample axes.
Variance as the driver, multiple or triple peaks, and disappearance under optimally tuned regularization are not tested. Early stopping, via best-epoch accuracy, is only touched on in Fig. 11.
There is no recounting of effective parameters.

missing.what: Best-epoch test accuracy versus sparsity, showing the double descent largely vanishes, with only a slight Critical-Phase drop
missing.locator: Figure 11; Section 4 'The best test accuracy benefits from pruning'

missing.what: Reinitialization versus lottery-ticket curves, where the peak shifts left

record.verdict_notes: The V1 linkage treats remaining parameter count under pruning as the model-size axis. The authors themselves frame the Critical Phase as 'around the interpolation threshold' and call the curve symmetric to deep double descent. A curator who requires width or depth scaling should move r1-r6 back to fits_no_version. All values are figure-only. The original sources are not this paper.

versions.untested_parts: Model size is not swept; pruning sparsity is the varied axis.
Training curves are shown, but the study does not test or report a fall-rise-fall curve over epochs.
Training sample size is not varied.
The study tests a sparsity sweep, not a capacity-increase sweep past an interpolation point across model classes.
The paper measures learning distance against sparsity, but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across size, epoch, and sample axes.
Tests synthetic label-noise dependence for sparse double descent only; does not test variance as the driver, multiple or triple peaks, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
The study does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether that converts a second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.operation_detail: Iteratively prune weights to increase sparsity, retraining between pruning steps.
rows.measure: Train and test accuracy as functions of sparsity
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard deviation; five runs with different seeds
rows.note: The authors describe test performance as first worsening, then improving, then worsening again as sparsity increases. This is sparse double descent, not the model-size curve in V1.
rows.check: Read along remaining-parameter count, the sparsity sweep is a capacity axis. The authors place the Critical Phase around the interpolation threshold, so the row bears on V1 in a new setting and should not be 'none'.

rows.operation_detail: Measure the L2 distance from original initialization to learned parameters across sparsity levels.
rows.measure: L2 learning distance and test accuracy versus sparsity
rows.note: The authors report that the distance curve correlates with the test-accuracy curve and that the turning point is usually consistent with a distance peak.
rows.check: This is a learning-distance correlate over the sparsity axis only. It is not V5's single complexity measure across size, epoch and sample axes. The authors state the correlation holds on MNIST, so the row is closer to observed than partial; either way it belongs under fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: Pruned LeNet-300-100, ResNet-18 and ResNet-101 (the last in Fig. 30, a declared left-out figure) with synthetic label noise (20-80%), under magnitude pruning and LTR retraining
relationships.reason: As remaining parameters grow, test accuracy rises, dips at the interpolation threshold (Critical Phase), then recovers (r1-r6). The authors report this as robust across pruning and retraining settings.
relationships.display_finding: As remaining parameters increased, test accuracy rose, dipped at interpolation, then recovered across the tested pruning and retraining settings.
